notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0579.tlg010.1st1K-gr: Both entries are excerpts the editor has stitched together from later writers; '. . .' marks the editor's omissions. '[der Götter]' in 13 is the editor's German gloss, 'of the gods', rendered as '[those of the gods]', and the words in angled brackets are an editor's supplement. In 12 the phrase 'the egg, conceived and conceiving the god' is uncertain in construction, and the clause beginning 'unless, indeed' is elliptical. The long sentence on Orpheus in 13 is a genitive construction with no main verb in the excerpt; it is rendered as a statement.

nodes.text: 12. The Theology recorded by the Peripatetic Eudemus as being Orpheus' passed over in silence the whole intelligible [order] . . . and made its beginning from Night, from whom Homer too, even if he has not made the genealogy continuous, starts; for we must not accept Eudemus when he says that Homer begins from Ocean and Tethys ['Ocean, origin of the gods, and mother Tethys']; for he evidently knows Night too as so very great a goddess that even Zeus reveres her: 'for he shrank from doing what would displease swift Night'. But let Homer too begin from Night. Hesiod, when he relates that Chaos came into being first, seems to me to have called the incomprehensible and wholly unified nature of the intelligible Chaos, and to bring forth Earth first from there, as a kind of beginning of the whole race of the gods; unless, indeed, [he means] Chaos as the second of the two principles, and Earth, Tartarus and Eros as the threefold intelligible, with Eros in place of the third, as [the intelligible] contemplated in its reversion. For Orpheus too names it so in the Rhapsodies . . . [In these Orphic Rhapsodies that are in circulation, then, the theology concerning the intelligible is something like this, as the philosophers also interpret it: in place of the one principle of all things they set Time; in place of the two, Aether and Chaos; in place of Being simply they reckon the Egg; and they make this the first triad. To the second belongs either the egg, conceived and conceiving the god, or the shining tunic, or the cloud, since from these Phanes leaps forth; for they philosophise differently at different times about the middle one . . . and to the third, Metis as intellect, Erikepaios as power, Phanes himself as father . . . Such is the customary Orphic theology. The arrangement we have given to the sphere, the Orphics say, is very like that in eggs: for the relation the shell has in the egg, the heaven has in the universe; and as the aether hangs in a circle from the heaven, so does the membrane from the shell.]

13. The [theology] handed down under the name of Hieronymus and Hellanicus, if indeed he is not the same man, runs thus: 'There was water,' he says, 'from the beginning, and matter, from which the earth was solidified', positing these two as first principles, water and earth . . . and that the third principle after the two was born from these, I mean water and earth, and was a serpent having heads of a bull and of a lion grown onto it, and in the middle the face of a god, and that it also had wings on its shoulders and was named unageing Time, and also Heracles. With him was Necessity, who is the same nature, and Adrasteia, incorporeal, her arms stretched out through the whole cosmos, touching its limits. This, I think, is said to be the third principle, standing in the place of substance, except that he made it male-female to show the cause that generates all things . . . This Time, the serpent, begets a threefold offspring: moist Aether, he says, and boundless Chaos, and third besides these misty Erebus . . . Further, in these Time begot an egg . . . and third besides these an incorporeal god with golden wings on his shoulders, who had bulls' heads grown onto his flanks, and on his head a monstrous serpent, appearing in all kinds of animal shapes . . . And this theology hymns Protogonos [the First-born] and calls him Zeus, orderer of all things and of the whole cosmos; therefore he is also called Pan. Orpheus, who first discovered their names [those of the gods] and went through their births and told what each of them had done, and who is believed among them to speak more truly about the gods, and whom Homer too follows in most things, especially concerning the gods, also establishes their first origin from water: 'Ocean, who was made the origin for all'. For according to him water was the beginning of all things; from the water mud settled; and from both was born a living creature, a serpent, with a lion's head grown onto it 〈and another, a bull's〉, and between them the face of a god, named Heracles and Time. This Heracles begot an enormous egg, which, filled out by the force of the one who begot it, broke in two from the friction. The part at its top was made to be Heaven, and the part carried downward Earth; and there came forth also a certain two-bodied god. Heaven, uniting with Earth, begets as females Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos, and as males the Hundred-handers Cottus, Gyges, Briareus, and the Cyclopes Brontes, Steropes and Arges; these he bound and cast down into Tartarus, having learned that he would be thrown out of his rule by his children. For this reason Earth in anger bore the Titans: 'And lady Earth bore sons to Heaven, whom indeed they call by the name of Titans, because they took vengeance on great starry Heaven.'
